transcript.reader:
Two questions, and a say-back to check first.

**Say-back:** you're claiming that Sholes' up-stroke typebars, which jam when struck in quick succession, forced him into a scrambled key order; that QWERTY then rode a thin early lead from the Remington deal; and that from the late 1880s touch typing, system scale economies and one-way typist retraining costs locked the industry onto it by the mid-1890s — so the board we have is an accident of sequencing held in place ever since, not the best of the alternatives. Is that a fair version, made as strong as you'd make it? And if I had to point at the one thing being explained, would I point at "the top row spells QWERTYUIOP", or at "the market settled on a single board rather than several"?

**1.** Name one change to the world between 1885 and 1905 that would have kept QWERTY from locking in. Then name one change in those same years that your account says would have made **no** difference to which board won.

**2.** Which part of your account breaks if QWERTY was not in fact the inferior board — that is, if the speed-typing records and the Navy retraining result don't hold up? If nothing in it breaks, which sentence of the paper is doing the work of "wrong system" rather than "the winner"?
transcript.author:
**Say-back.** Broadly fair, with three emendations. First, the explanandum. The one thing I am explaining is the *singleness* — that the market settled on one arrangement and stayed there. "QWERTYUIOP" is the instance that lets me tell the story, not the theory. Second, "accident" is too weak a word for what I mean: I mean temporally remote, essentially random and transient events magnified by expectations (Katz-Shapiro, Hanson) and by the generalized Polya-urn dynamics. Third, I would not have written "accident of sequencing *not inferiority*" quite so flatly. I do call it the wrong system, but the paper also says the story is "simply illustrative" and that how much of the world works this way is "an open empirical issue." And the jam story is not mine to assert as engineering fact: it is Sholes' trial-and-error, plus Remington's mechanics finishing the job — including the R that made TYPE WRITER one-row typable. So: yes, that is my version, made as strong as I would make it, with the caveat that the illustrative-status sentence is load-bearing.

**1.** A change that would have prevented lock-in: the early appearance of a *concentrated* trainer who internalized the externality — a very large employer, a public school system, or a manufacturers' standards agreement committed to a non-QWERTY board before the stock of QWERTY-specific touch-typing skill accumulated. My whole asymmetry rests on trainers being numerous, small, and unwilling to fund general human capital. Concentrate that, and QWERTY's slender lead never becomes self-reinforcing.

A change in those years that would have made no difference: curing the typebar jam. Down-stroke, front-stroke, Crandall's sleeve, Hammond, Blickensderfer's DHIATENSOR — I say so myself: the industry moved to "the Universal" precisely when the micro-technological rationale for QWERTY was being removed by engineering progress. Hardware conversion costs were falling; that freed makers and left the software side, plus expectations, to decide. Better machines, cheaper machines, a visible printing point, even a more sensible default layout — none of those select among eligible candidates.

**2.** The sentence doing that work is Section III: competition without perfect futures markets "drove the industry prematurely into standardization on the wrong system." Section I's "this superior design" presupposes it; the speed records and the Navy amortization result are what make "wrong" credible — and I know both were later contested (Liebowitz and Margolis), so treat them as claims, not proofs.

What breaks if they fail is the welfare indictment, not the mechanism. Technical interrelatedness, system scale economies, one-way software conversion, non-convergence to a fixed-point distribution — the urn still converges with probability one to *some* color; nothing guarantees the good one. That is a claim about indeterminacy and history-dependence, not about the winner being second-best. I would lose the "quiet terrors" and keep the path dependence. I leaned harder on Dvorak than the argument required.

transcript.reader:
Good. Two more.

**1.** Remove Sholes' jam problem entirely — and with it the "wrong system" sentence and the Navy result. For the question we've frozen — why one arrangement and not several — which job stops getting done? If the answer is none, then the jam story is colour for *this* question: is it there to do a different one, and which?

**2.** Your urn converges to one colour because the setup says returns are increasing without bound. What holds that part in place for 1890s typing — what reading would show the returns flatten out (a small lead stops paying, several boards coexist), and is there a reading on your list that should show they don't?

The blank is itself an answer; I'll put it to you plainer, and add one.

**1.** Make the assumption concrete. In 1895, for one pair of boards: as the number of machines on a given board rose, what fell? Name the quantity — a trainer's fee, an operator's wage premium, an employer's hiring time — and say where in the record we would see it falling, and where we would see it stop falling. If there is nowhere we would see either, then "increasing without bound" is asserted rather than held, and I'll mark it so.

**2.** Suppose the 1895–1905 record had shown three or four boards coexisting, each with its own trained pool, no single one dominant. Would you have written this paper? What would have had to be different in the world for that to happen, and how would we see it in the record — sizing of firms, training schools, a standards agreement, something else?
transcript.author:
**1.** I accept the mark. The quantity I need is the fee for instruction in touch typing, or equivalently the employer's cost of matching machine to operator — the premium he pays for a pre-trained QWERTY typist over retraining one, or over buying a non-QWERTY machine plus training. Where we would see it falling: commercial-school tuitions and curricula, the relative price of "the Universal" against the Ideal, want ads specifying board, and the disappearance of the DHIATENSOR home row from catalog copy. Where we would see it stop falling: after standardization — and that is the difficulty. Once one pool remains there is no comparison set, so the falling returns become unobservable exactly when they are supposed to have done their work. What I actually have in the record is indirect and thin: manufacturers offering "the Universal" as an option, the absence of employer-funded retraining, and the Navy doing what private employers would not. The Navy result was my one quantitative reading of conversion cost. Strip it and "unbounded" is asserted, not held. So mark it — as illustrative-and-unmeasured rather than as a measured finding.

**2.** If three or four boards coexisted, I would not have written this paper; I would have written the paper that asks why *that* equilibrium was stable. What would have to differ: returns that flatten — training pools small enough to be self-sustaining, and partitioned markets. Concretely, large vertically integrated employers running in-house typing schools, which internalize what a competitive market does not; or makers committed by agreement to proprietary boards; or genuinely distinct task demands, stenography versus general office typing, sustaining separate pools. We would see it in the record as sustained parallel catalog offerings rather than the Ideal vanishing into an option, as school curricula persisting side by side, and as placement-bureau or want-ad data showing skills that did not travel. What my paper's contrast between "the Universal" and the Ideal cannot rule out is that it is n=1.

transcript.reader:
Two more, then I'll write it up.

**1.** Section III claims "many more QWERTY worlds lying out there." That is a claim about other industries, not about keyboards. Name one case where your three ingredients were plainly present and several standards persisted instead of one — or say plainly that you know of none. Then: if such a case turned up, what in your account would have to give — the ingredients, or "returns increasing without bound"?

**2.** Which of your parts came from the keyboard record and which were already in your hands? Specifically: did you have technical interrelatedness, system scale economies and quasi-irreversibility as a package before you looked at the 1890s market, or did the 1890s market supply them? And name plainly what is on loan — from Veblen's railway wagons, from Arthur's urn, from Katz–Shapiro and Hanson on expectations — since I'll mark those as borrowed and say by whom.
transcript.author:
**1.** Plainly: I know of none that I could document as cleanly as this one. The near-cases I would point to are railway gauges, where break-of-gauge costs are exactly the compatibility effect, yet broad and standard gauge coexisted in Britain for decades until 1892; and screw threads, Whitworth versus SAE, which persisted until the 1948 agreements. Both have a feature the keyboard lacks: geographic or institutional segmentation that truncates the pool. So they are not really counterexamples to the mechanism — they are counterexamples to its unrestricted application. If a genuine case turned up, the ingredients survive and the *unboundedness* goes. Increasing returns that saturate at some finite pool size yield a process with more than one stable point, and that is precisely Arthur's later refinement. I would rather concede the assumption than the ingredients, because the ingredients are ordinary economics; unboundedness is the strong claim I am least able to measure — as I conceded in the last answer.

**2.** The package was in my hands before the 1890s market. Technical interrelatedness, scale economies and quasi-irreversibility are what I had been arguing about ridge-and-furrow and about nineteenth-century American factor prices and labor-saving bias; those are cited in the paper as my own earlier scribblings. What the keyboard record supplied was the *timing asymmetry* — hardware conversion costs falling while software conversion costs rose — and the employers-refuse-to-fund-general-training observation. I would defend that asymmetry as the paper's own contribution.

On loan, plainly: Veblen's "penalties of taking the lead" and the undersized railway wagons; Arthur for the generalized Polya urn, the non-ergodic convergence result, and the 1983 model of technological competition — I say in the note that only some of my debt to him is recorded. Katz-Shapiro and Hanson lend the expectations-and-network externality support. And the Dvorak speed records and the Navy amortization figure came to me through the Dvorak advocacy literature, not from independent testing; that is the loan I would least want to stand behind.

transcript.reader:
Last two.

**1.** Your nearest rival, I take it, is: QWERTY won because it was, all things considered, the better-supported choice, and the Dvorak studies are wrong. Since you've let go of the welfare sentence and kept the mechanism, name one reading in the 1890s record that would come out differently under your account than under that rival. If there is none, then at the level of "why one board", the two are the same explanation, and the difference sits in a question you're not answering.

**2.** Pull. If expectations alone can lock a market in — Katz–Shapiro style, buy the board you think others will buy — what does the rising cost of software conversion still do? Take it out and keep expectations plus scale economies: does the urn still converge? If it does, which of the two gives way at the joints, and where would the record show you've drawn the line in the wrong place?
transcript.author:
**1.** The cleanest discriminator is counterfactual — whether the winner would have differed had the Remington lead gone to Crandall or the Ideal — and we cannot observe it. So let me name the one reading that leans, then concede your point.

That reading is whether the Ideal and the Hammond failed *as machines* or as *compatible software*. Put the record under that line: if non-QWERTY machines were engineering-competitive and lost only because the trained pool was QWERTY, that is my signature — a good machine losing to the established pool. But the rival absorbs it immediately, because "better supported" is exactly what he is claiming, network included. So the reading separates the mechanisms only if "better supported" is restricted to hardware merit, and it is not.

Hence, yes: at the level of "why one board," we are giving substantially the same explanation, and we differ only on whether the standard was merited — the welfare question I have conceded I cannot settle from this record. The evidence that would discriminate is counterfactual sensitivity to a slender initial lead, and I have no archival substitute for it. That is a real limit of the paper, not a rhetorical one.

**2.** Pull quasi-irreversibility and keep expectations plus scale economies: yes, the urn still converges. Katz-Shapiro tipping does not require sunk skills; expectations alone will select. So convergence is not the job irreversibility is doing.

What it does is *persistence* — that the winner, once in, cannot be dislodged. Selection by expectations and scale economies; lock-in by rising conversion costs. Sever that joint and the model still picks a colour but should not keep it, and I should expect flips: a coordinated purchaser wanting the other board would simply retrain. A century of stasis then needs a different keeper — sunk hardware, or nobody coordinating the flip.

And the record may already show I drew the line wrong. My Navy figure — ten days to amortize retraining — is my evidence of waste; it is equally evidence that conversion is *cheap* for an employer. The same number that indicts the standard argues against the irreversibility that supposedly holds it. I cannot have it both ways, and I did not notice the tension when I wrote it.

# Report: David, "Clio and the Economics of QWERTY" (1985)

## 1. The question, frozen

**What is explained:** the *singleness* — that the US typewriter market settled on one keyboard arrangement and stayed there. The owner said this himself: "QWERTYUIOP" is the instance that lets him tell the story, not the theory. **Range:** the US market, Sholes' patents to about 1905, with the standard held to the present. **Kind:** what produced it — forward, from causes. Two things sit outside the freeze and are marked separately: why *this* arrangement rather than another, and whether the standard was merited.

## 2. The parts, in the owner's words

P1 Sholes' typebars jam when struck fast; the keyboard was rearranged by trial and error, finished by Remington's mechanics. P2 A thin, precarious early lead (under ~5,000 US machines by 1880). P3 Touch typing arrives in the late 1880s, adapted to the Remington QWERTY board — the "software". P4 Technical interrelatedness: machine and typist's memory must be compatible. P5 System scale economies: user costs fall as a board's pool grows; a generalized Polya urn. P6 Expectations magnify a slender lead (Katz–Shapiro, Hanson). P7 Quasi-irreversibility: software conversion costs rising while hardware conversion costs fall — he calls this the paper's own contribution. P8 Trainers are numerous, small, won't fund general human capital. P9 "Historical accidents" with great leverage; unbounded increasing returns; convergence to one colour with probability one. P10 Section III: "prematurely into standardization on the wrong system"; "many more QWERTY worlds".

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | By what, or what would settle it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 jam | **Idle** | His own poke: cure the jam and the outcome is unchanged — down-stroke, front-stroke, Crandall's sleeve, Edison's wheel, the Ideal board all lost anyway, as the engineering rationale was being removed. Removed singly and with P2; it does work on the *other* question — why the row reads as it does. |
| P2 thin lead | **Held** | By the magnification job: expectations and the urn need a lead; the sales record supplies it. |
| P3 touch typing | **Held** | By the singleness job: no software, no pool, no lock-in. The 1880s date is the hinge. |
| P4 interrelatedness, P5 scale economies | **Borrowed** | In his words, the package he already had from the ridge-and-furrow and factor-price work (David 1971, 1975), plus Arthur's urn. Not tested here. |
| P6 expectations | **Borrowed** | Katz–Shapiro, Hanson. It also does the *selection* job alone: remove P7 and the urn still converges. |
| P7 irreversibility | **Held if** | The only part that keeps the winner in place ("selection by expectations and scale; lock-in by rising conversion costs"). The job is in doubt: the one number offered — the Navy's ten days to amortize retraining — is equally evidence conversion was cheap. No reading was named that shows a willing purchaser unable to flip. Settle it with want-ad or placement data on trained operators after standardization. |
| P8 small trainers | **Held**, weakly | By his own counterfactual: concentrate the trainers — one big employer, a school system, a standards agreement committed before the QWERTY pool formed — and the lead never self-reinforces. A stated comparison, not an observed case; historical parts hold less tightly. |
| P9 unboundedness / "accidents" | **Unknown**, and **catch-all** | "Unbounded" is conceded as unmeasured: the fall in learner cost is unobservable exactly when it did its work, because one pool leaves no comparison set. "Accidents" names no events, so it can absorb any failure. Needed gauge: one quantity that fell as a board's pool grew — school tuitions, the price of "the Universal" against the Ideal, want ads naming a board. |
| P10 "wrong system"; "more QWERTY worlds" | **Borrowed**; **Loose** | Rests on Dvorak advocacy literature and the Navy figure — he named this as the loan he'd least stand behind (contested by Liebowitz–Margolis) — and answers the welfare question, not the frozen one. The "many worlds" claim names no case; his two near-cases (railway gauges, Whitworth vs SAE) show the ingredients *without* one winner, and differ by segmentation. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** Had three or four boards coexisted, he says he would have written a different paper. A good answer — and it exposes that "unbounded returns" was doing the flip's work: saturating returns give more than one stable point (Arthur's own later refinement).

**Direction.** Mostly forward. But the reading that would carry the mechanism — falling returns — has no measurement window.

**Answer in the starting points.** Partly yes. The urn converges to one colour because unbounded increasing returns are written into the setup, so singleness is in the starting point. He conceded this, and chose to keep the ingredients and drop the assumption.

**Jobs, and where they came from.** J1 singleness — given by him. J2 why this arrangement — given by the title but reclassified by him as the instance. J3 why it persisted a century — given. J4 why not in gauges and threads — added by me; he answered it.

**Pairs that pull.** P6 against P7: selection versus persistence. He drew the line there and named the sign that it is drawn wrongly: the Navy figure indicts the standard and undercuts the irreversibility in the same breath. P10 pulls against P7 the same way.

**Rival.** "It won because it was better supported, network included." He conceded no 1890s reading separates the two mechanisms unless "better supported" is confined to hardware merit — which is not his rival's claim. So at the level of *why one board*, the two are the same explanation; the difference lives in the welfare question, which he says the record cannot settle. Test run on rival and on the innocent neighbour; both pass.

**Where the parts came from.** Built: the timing asymmetry (hardware conversion costs falling, software rising) and employers' refusal to fund training. Fitted and carried over: the three-ingredient package. Asserted: unboundedness, "many more QWERTY worlds", the Dvorak and Navy figures.

**Change list.** Concentrated trainers — would have mattered (no lock-in). Jam cured — no difference. Saturating returns — would have mattered. A coordinated purchaser wanting to flip — matters if P7 holds, nothing if it doesn't. What is left out was said up front: "simply illustrative"; "an open empirical issue".

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

A gauge for the unboundedness — one measurable quantity that fell as a board's pool grew, with a reading that would have worried him. Second: the gauges-and-threads case, with the segmentation difference written down before looking.

## 6. What this does not show

Not truth or falsity, and nothing about whether the standard was merited.

## 7. One next step

Write down, before searching, what want-ad or placement data would look like in 1900 if a coordinated purchaser could have flipped. Then look.
transcript.author:
The audit is fairer to the paper than the paper is to itself, and I would sign most of it. Three things I would enter.

First, on P1: I agree it is idle for the frozen question, and I said as much when pressed. But "colour" undersells it. The jam is what makes the instance teachable — it is why the row reads QWERTYUIOP, it is why the story has a villain and a name, and the title is the jam. I keep it for the same reason Veblen kept the undersized wagons.

Second, on P6/P7: I would resist the phrasing that expectations "select alone, so irreversibility is idle." Selection without persistence gives churn, not a standard — and the frozen question is not "why did one colour lead" but "why did it stay." P7 is idle for convergence and load-bearing for the thing being explained. That said, I conceded the joint and the Navy figure, and I do not retract the concession.

Third, on P9's catch-all charge: accepted. "Accidents" naming no events is a real defect; it can absorb any disconfirmation. The gauges-and-threads comparison should have been in the paper as the boundary case.

The next step is the right one. Prediction to write down first: if coordinated purchasers could flip, post-1900 want ads should show board-neutral hiring, and they should not name QWERTY. If they do name it, P7 holds a bit longer.
